name: Hebrew (Modern, with a bridge to Biblical)

chat.name: everyday Modern Israeli Hebrew (write with niqqud on new or hard words)

translit.name: Israeli romanisation: kh = ח/כ (as in 'Bach'), ts = צ, ' = a break (א/ע); the accented vowel is stressed

frequency.source: FrequencyWords by Hermit Dave (OpenSubtitles 2018, Hebrew), CC BY-SA 4.0
frequency.note: Subtitle Hebrew is everyday spoken-style Modern Hebrew, so this estimates coverage of conversation and TV.

notes.title: Modern first, Biblical later
body: This pack teaches **Modern Israeli Hebrew** for speaking, listening, reading and writing. Unit 12 is a bridge to **Biblical Hebrew**: the vav-consecutive (וַיֹּאמֶר 'and he said'), older word order, and Genesis 1:1–5 in the original.
Modern and Biblical Hebrew share the alphabet, roots and most core vocabulary, so nothing you learn now is wasted.

notes.title: Your Arabic helps (and vice versa)
body: Hebrew and Arabic are sister Semitic languages. Most roots line up with regular sound correspondences: Arabic **s** often = Hebrew **sh** (salām / shalom, samiʕa / shama 'hear'), Arabic **ḍ/ṣ** = Hebrew **ts** (ʔarḍ / erets 'land'), Arabic **th** = Hebrew **sh** (thalātha / shalosh 'three').
Words with a shared root show a 🔗 link to the Arabic word. The root-and-pattern idea you learned in Arabic Unit 5 works the same way here (binyanim and mishkalim).

notes.title: ח and כ sound the same
body: In standard Israeli Hebrew, ח and כ (without a dot) are both pronounced kh as in 'Bach', and א and ע are both a soft catch or silent. The spelling preserves older sounds that Arabic still has (ح ḥ, ع ʕ), and many Mizrahi speakers still pronounce them.
So the sound training here practises the contrasts that matter for understanding Israelis: kh vs h, the uvular r vs kh, and k vs kh.

notes.title: Niqqud on and off
body: Learners' texts add vowel points (niqqud); Israeli newspapers, signs and phones don't. Keep niqqud on at first, then switch it off in Settings to practise real reading. Unpointed spelling uses ו and י as vowel letters (ktiv male), so words look slightly different: שָׁלוֹם → שלום, סִפְרִיָּה → ספרייה.

notes.title: Typing Hebrew on iPhone
body: Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard → Hebrew (free). Typed answers are matched without niqqud, and final letters (ם ן ך ף ץ) are treated like their normal forms.

notes.title: Unverified content
body: All sentences and vowel pointing were written by Claude and are marked unverified. Niqqud in particular is easy to get slightly wrong. Tap ⚑ Flag error on anything suspicious.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 1: א ב ג ד ה ו
scriptLessons.note: Hebrew is written right to left, with consonants only; vowels are optional dots and dashes (niqqud). Letters don't join.

letters.name: álef
letters.sound: Silent or a soft catch; carries a vowel. (Arabic ا / ء)

letters.name: bet / vet
letters.sound: With a dot inside: b. Without: v.

letters.name: gímel
letters.sound: Hard g as in 'go'.

letters.name: dálet
letters.sound: d.

letters.name: hey
letters.sound: Light h; often silent at the end of a word, where it marks a vowel (-a / -e).

letters.name: vav
letters.sound: v, or the vowels o (וֹ) and u (וּ). Also the word 'and' (וְ-) attached to the next word.

scriptLessons.title: Letters 2: ז ח ט י כ ך ל
scriptLessons.note: Five letters have a special final form at the end of a word. The first one is ך (final khaf).

letters.name: záyin
letters.sound: z.

letters.name: khet
letters.sound: kh as in 'Bach' (originally pharyngeal ḥ, like Arabic ح).

letters.name: tet
letters.sound: t (originally emphatic, like Arabic ط).

letters.name: yud
letters.sound: y, or the vowel i / e. The smallest letter.

letters.name: kaf / khaf
letters.sound: With a dot: k. Without: kh (same sound as ח). ך is the final form.

letters.name: lámed
letters.sound: l. The tallest letter. Also the prefix 'to' (לְ-).

scriptLessons.title: Letters 3: מ ם נ ן ס ע
scriptLessons.note: Two more final forms: ם (final mem) and ן (final nun).

letters.name: mem
letters.sound: m. ם at the end of a word. Also the prefix 'from' (מִ-).

letters.name: nun
letters.sound: n. ן at the end of a word.

letters.name: sámekh
letters.sound: s.

letters.name: áyin
letters.sound: Silent or a soft catch in most Israeli speech (originally ʕ, like Arabic ع).

scriptLessons.title: Letters 4: פ ף צ ץ ק ר ש ת
scriptLessons.note: The last two final forms: ף and ץ. ש has two sounds, marked by a dot on the right (sh) or left (s).

letters.name: pey / fey
letters.sound: With a dot: p. Without: f. ף is final.

letters.name: tsádi
letters.sound: ts as in 'cats' (originally emphatic ṣ, like Arabic ص). ץ is final.

letters.name: kuf
letters.sound: k: same sound as כּ (originally q, like Arabic ق).

letters.name: resh
letters.sound: Uvular r in the back of the throat, like French or German r (a voiced kh).

letters.name: shin / sin
letters.sound: Dot on the right: sh. Dot on the left: s.

letters.name: tav
letters.sound: t. Often marks feminine words (-et, -it, -ut).

scriptLessons.title: Niqqud: the vowel points
scriptLessons.note: Most Hebrew you'll see has no niqqud, so learn the points but don't depend on them. Toggle niqqud in Settings.

letters.name: pátakh, kamats
letters.sound: A line (pátakh) or a small T (kamats) under the letter: a.

letters.name: segól, tseré
letters.sound: Three dots (segól) or two dots side by side (tseré) under the letter: e.

letters.name: khírik
letters.sound: One dot under the letter (often followed by י): i.

letters.name: khólam
letters.sound: A dot above the top left, or וֹ: o.

letters.name: kubúts, shurúk
letters.sound: Three slanted dots (kubúts) or וּ (shurúk): u.

letters.name: shva
letters.sound: Two dots stacked under the letter: a short e, or no vowel at all.

letters.name: dagésh
letters.sound: A dot inside ב כ פ makes them hard (b, k, p). Without it: v, kh, f.

contrasts.title: ח/כ kh vs ה h
contrasts.note: ח and כ sound the same (kh); ה is a plain h.

contrasts.title: ר r vs ח/כ kh
contrasts.note: Both are made at the back of the throat; r has voice (buzz), kh doesn't.

speaking.en: Introduce yourself: name, where you're from, how you are.
Say what you study, where, and which languages you speak.
Order a drink and something to eat, and ask the price.
Describe what you do every day.
Tell what you did yesterday, in order.
Describe your family: who, how old, where they live.
Ask the price of three things at the shuk and bargain.
Tell a doctor what hurts and since when.
Give directions from your dorm to the library.
Say what you will do this weekend and what you need to do.
Explain why you're learning Hebrew and Arabic together.
Read Genesis 1:3 aloud, then retell verses 1–5 in Modern Hebrew.
